rv.q: But it’s a remarkable end to an extraordinary play.

It’s bracing to see someone use the stage with such emphatic intent to provoke discourse, and Rodrigues draws on writers as varied as Aeschylus, Lorca, Brecht and Shaw to work up his unique, disturbing brew.
A striking premise, then, but as happens in the story itself, it feels as though the execution itself gets botched.
To the credit of this extraordinary and so, so timely production, I'm now further away than ever from knowing if it's if or when and then comes the even more terrifying interrogative, how?
This remains urgent, provocative stuff – exactly the sort of thing the National should be programming.
This production is nuanced, unsettling and thoughtful.
It’s a tough and drawn-out watch in sections, but has there ever been a more contentious and apposite vehicle for the times in which we live?
But there’s an uncomfortable sense that by setting out to trigger a reaction, it is a little too sure of its own importance.

cn.t: Rodrigues' provocative Portuguese import about killing fascists divides critics as urgent and powerful versus uncomfortable and simplistic, though most agree it's deliberately designed to unsettle and spark debate.
